clue.text: Disorderly actors appearing plastered

parts.note: rough can mean unruly or disorderly, as in rough behaviour
the actors in a play are collectively its cast

explanation.surface: Unruly performers turn up on stage drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastered' looks like slang for drunk, but here it describes a wall coated in rough plaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughcast is a coarse plaster of lime and gravel, so a wall finished with it is plastered.

clue.text: A way of learning by repetition around university

indicators.note: the word for learning by repetition goes around the letter for university

parts.note: rote learning is memorising by repetition

explanation.surface: Learning things by heart is a method used at college.
explanation.definitionFit: A route is a road or course taken, so a path or way.

clue.text: Liberate one soul in torment

indicators.note: something in torment is twisted and racked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A suffering spirit is to be set free.
explanation.definitionFit: To unloose is to unfasten or release, a synonym for freeing.

clue.text: Doesn't take kindly to making haste

indicators.note: making means forming or constructing, so these letters are made into another word

explanation.surface: Someone dislikes being hurried.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe something is to dislike it, the opposite of taking kindly to it.

clue.text: They travel to work and learn in France at the Paris assembly

definitions.text: They travel to work and learn

parts.note: au is French for at the, as in au revoir

indicators.note: assembly is putting parts together, so these letters are assembled in a new order

explanation.surface: Young people travel to work and study at a Paris gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural phrase fits 'They': these are young foreigners who live with a family, look after the children, and learn the language.
explanation.definitionFit: Au pairs are young people who go abroad to do childcare while learning the language.

clue.text: Dumped, though given a warning

definitions.meaning: ... means emptied out or knocked over, like rubbish ... a cart
alerted in advance with secret information

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both emptied off something and warned in advance, two separate idioms.

clue.text: Lively betting at the track

parts.note: SP is the starting price, the odds in horse-race betting
RY is short for railway, a track for trains

explanation.surface: Someone is energetically placing bets at the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: SP, the starting price, is the official odds offered at a British racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry is a synonym for active and nimble, usually said of an older person.

clue.text: Something that's essential when raising fruit

indicators.note: in a down clue raising lifts the letters so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: something essential is a must, here with its article: a must
as can mean when, as in as I left

explanation.surface: A vital ingredient is needed when growing fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' turns A MUST AS backwards, which suits a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a kind of mandarin orange, a small citrus fruit.

clue.text: The opportune moment? Watch for it!

definitions.meaning: a watch is made to show the ...

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both the proper moment and the accurate hour a watch should show.

clue.text: Period added to the end of a sentence

definitions.meaning: period is the American name for the dot that closes a sentence

definitions.text: added to the end of a sentence
definitions.meaning: the dot is the mark placed after the last word of a sentence

explanation.definitionFit: British usage names the dot ending a sentence this way where Americans say period.

clue.text: Got pea soup? Yes!

indicators.note: a soup is a mixture or mess, so these letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A diner is delighted to be served pea soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soup' signals rearranging GOT PEA, and the whole clue also describes the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Potage is the French word for a thick soup, which pea soup certainly is.

clue.text: No rest in assembly for these choir members

indicators.note: assembly means putting parts together, so these letters are assembled in a new order

explanation.surface: Singers complain they get no break when gathered together.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenors are the high male voices that sing in a choir.

clue.text: Injustice in the players' union

parts.note: Equity is the British trade union for actors, who are players

explanation.surface: Unfair treatment is going on within the actors' union.
explanation.walkthrough: EQUITY is the name of the UK actors' union, and players here means actors, not sportspeople.
explanation.definitionFit: Inequity is unfairness, the opposite of equity, so it is a synonym for injustice.

clue.text: Doing nothing right in an exam

indicators.note: the letter for right is placed inside the phrase for an exam

parts.note: an exam is a test, here with its article: a test

explanation.surface: A student sits idle, being correct during a test.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at rest is to be still and idle, the state of doing nothing.

clue.text: Fair distribution of beer to all

indicators.note: distributing something spreads it around, so these letters are shared out in a new order

explanation.surface: Handing out beer to everyone is only fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair in the sense of middling or passable is a synonym of acceptable.

clue.text: Stand for serving soldiers

parts.note: soldiers are strips of toast for dipping in egg, so a stand serving them holds toast; the surface suggests a tribute to troops

explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers are British nursery slang for thin fingers of toast dipped into a boiled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: A rack holding slices of toast upright is a stand for serving them at breakfast.

clue.text: Picadors get injured now and then

indicators.note: being injured means being damaged or bent out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The horsemen in a bullfight are hurt from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: Picadors are the horsemen who lance the bull in a bullfight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sporadic happens irregularly, occurring only now and then.

clue.text: In second part of race, sprint recklessly

parts.note: a lap is one circuit of a track, part of a race
a dash is a short sprint

explanation.surface: A runner charges carelessly on the second circuit of a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapdash describes something done hastily and carelessly, in a reckless manner.

clue.text: Fish cake?

definitions.meaning: a fish of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
a ... cake is a small liquorice sweet from Pontefract in Yorkshire

explanation.walkthrough: Pomfret cakes are small round liquorice sweets from Pontefract in Yorkshire; the question mark admits they are not really cakes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a sea fish and a small liquorice lozenge called a cake.

clue.text: Be frugal, mate!

definitions.meaning: to ... resources is to manage them thriftily
a mate is a spouse, here a married man

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to use sparingly, and the noun is a married partner.

clue.text: He comes across as a false friend

indicators.note: false means not true to form, so these letters are changed into another order

explanation.surface: Someone turns out to be a disloyal companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes across' is read literally: the definition is someone who comes across things.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who discovers or chances upon something is the one who found it.

clue.text: Without breaks? Without brakes!

definitions.meaning: something without breaks goes on continuously with no pauses
a vehicle without brakes cannot halt

explanation.definitionFit: The word means continuous and also, read literally, unable to halt at all.

clue.text: Prefers French word in prose version

indicators.note: the French word sits within the reworked letters of prose
a version of something is a different rendering, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: mot is the French for word

explanation.surface: A writer opts for a French term in a prose translation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prefers' is used in its old sense of promoting someone to office, not liking one thing more.
explanation.definitionFit: To prefer someone in the old sense is to advance them in rank, which is to raise them up.

clue.text: Old sofa provides a rest in church

indicators.note: the article and the word for rest go inside the letters for church

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a nap is a short rest

explanation.surface: An antique couch offers a place to sit in church.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Old sofa': canapé once meant a sofa, as it still does in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Canapé is an old word for a couch or settee, borrowed from French, long before it meant a snack.

clue.text: Miss part of a declaration

indicators.note: part of signals that a run of letters is taken from inside the words a declaration

explanation.surface: Someone misses part of a statement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a verb but it is the title for a girl or woman; the definition is a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Clara is a woman's name, and a Miss is an unmarried girl or woman.

clue.text: Coming before a superior

definitions.meaning: the head of a priory, a religious superior

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means earlier, and the noun is the monk in charge of a priory.

clue.text: A brie I ordered in Spain and Portugal

indicators.note: ordered means arranged, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A diner orders a French cheese while holidaying in the peninsula.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iberian peninsula is the land mass occupied by these two countries.

clue.text: It's equipped for dispatching stock

parts.note: dispatching means killing and stock means livestock, though the surface suggests a warehouse sending goods out

explanation.definitionFit: A slaughterhouse is where livestock are killed for meat.

clue.text: Payment made to leading thespian for walk-on parts?

parts.note: a fee is a payment for services

indicators.note: leading picks the front letter of the word thespian

explanation.surface: An actor in a minor non-speaking role gets paid.
explanation.walkthrough: Walk-on parts are tiny roles, but read literally they are the parts you walk on.
explanation.definitionFit: The body parts a person walks on are the lower extremities at the end of the legs.

clue.text: Child sent to head, one breaking the rules

parts.note: a kid is a child
napper is old British slang for the head

explanation.surface: A pupil is sent to the headteacher for misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: NAPPER is dated British slang for the head; 'sent to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An abductor commits a serious crime, so is certainly someone breaking the law.
